 PUBLIC COMMENT RULES
 “(California Government Code Section 54954.3).
 (a) Every agenda for regular meetings shall provide an opportunity for members of the
 public to directly address the legislative body on any item of interest to the public, before
 or during the legislative body’s consideration of the item, that is within the subject matter
 jurisdiction of the legislative body, provided that no action shall be taken on any item not
 appearing on the agenda unless the action is otherwise authorized by subdivision (b) of
 Section 54954.2 [section omitted].

 (b) (1) The legislative body of a local agency may adopt reasonable regulations to ensure
 that the intent of the subdivision (a) is carried out, including, but not limited to, regulations
 limiting the total amount of time allocated for public testimony on particular issues and for
 each individual speaker.
  (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), when the legislative body of a local agency limits

  time for public comment, the legislative body of a local agency shall provide at least twice
 the allotted time to a member of the public who utilizes a translator to ensure that non-
 English speakers receive the same opportunity to directly address the legislative body of
 a local agency.”

 In furtherance of Section 54954.3 of the Brown Act, the public is allotted to speak a total
 of two (2) minutes on the entirety of the Consent Calendar(s), Appointment(s), New
 Business and Closed Session, with two (2) minutes on each Public Hearing, and, if
 desired, an additional two (2) minutes on items not on the agenda that are within the
 subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council. As specified in the Brown Act, a speaker
 utilizing a translator will receive twice the amount of time specified.

SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MONTHLY AND QUARTERLY
  INVESTMENT ACTIVITY REPORT FOR DECEMBER 2023

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council receive and file the monthly and quarterly
investment activity reports for the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency for December
2023.
BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Section 16 of the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency Investment
Policy, the City Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on
investments to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The
reports shall detail the type of investment, name of the issuer, purchase date, date of
maturity, amount of deposit, and rate of interest. This information shall be provided for
all City and Successor Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of
Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts, and
Community Facilities District accounts, which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly investment reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the City
of Palmdale and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations. The interest rates
presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable sources of market prices.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly and Quarterly Investment Reports
February 7, 2024
Page 2

DISCUSSION
Compliance with Investment Policy

For December, the invested portfolio amount for the City of Palmdale totaled
$306,405,140, an increase of $277,072 from the previous month, and an increase of
$34,299,142 compared to last year. The monthly increase is primarily the result of gains
in maturities.

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of December was $6,976,565. The
balance decreased by $978,537 from last month due to debt service payments made
during the month.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities, and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entities’ investment policies to 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements; and
3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on is providing liquidity to measure up
to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Division is currently investing in two pooled funds, Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF)
and California Asset Management Program (CAMP). These are intended for daily
operational activities and used for economic uncertainties and maintenance needs. The
pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the City and Successor Agency
meet cash flow requirements.

The total LAIF balance for the City of Palmdale at the end of December is $128,703,931.
No change from the prior month.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of December was $6,215,832. No change
from the prior month.

CAMP’s balance for City of Palmdale at the end of December was $266,599 compared
to November balance of $265,347. The slight increase is due to interest earned during
the month.

Re: Monthly and Quarterly Investment Reports
February 7, 2024
Page 3

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report. As of December 31, 2023, the interest rates for LAIF and CAMP investments
were at 3.929 percent and 5.55 percent, respectively. By comparison, the LAIF and
CAMP interest rates at the end of November were 3.843 percent and 5.58 percent. Both
rates have slightly increased within this month. This time last year, LAIF and CAMP
rates were at 2.173 percent and 4.30, respectively.

The chart above shows the Local Agency Investment Fund and California Asset
Management Program’s average monthly yields beginning March 2023 through
December 2023. The difference between the performance of the two funds is partly due
to the varying pool characteristics. CAMP's portfolio composition is more prone to
market volatility, resulting in performance variations.

Diversity

The Finance Division aims to diversify the investment portfolios to avoid incurring
unreasonable and avoidable risks regarding specific security types or individual financial
institutions.

The City of Palmdale and Successor Agency’s investment portfolios remain strongly
diversified. The monthly and quarterly report includes all investments held by both
entities and current book values as of December 31, 2023.

It is anticipated that the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency will have sufficient
sums of money to meet their expenditure requirements for the next six months. The
Finance Division will continue to monitor current economic conditions and the impact on
interest rates.

STRATEGIC PLAN

  health.
  C. Involve and expand engagement to enhance public oversight and
  transparency.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Requisition No. 240740 with Warren-Anderson Ford, Inc. for the purchase
  of one Roadline Model GPMT Graffiti Removal Truck in an amount not to exceed
  $156,947; and,
  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to approve the requisition and
  resulting purchase order with Warren-Anderson Ford, Inc., including minimal
  and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND
Graffiti is one of the leading issues reported to the City’s Maintenance Division. Last
fiscal year, more than 2,900 work orders were completed, resulting in 407,092 square
feet of graffiti removal at over 4,400 locations citywide. From July to December 2023,
work orders and square footage increased by 50%, with incident locations up by 70%.
This year is on trend to exceed Fiscal Year 2022-2023 totals.

The Graffiti Abatement team consists of three full-time technicians and two part-time
staff. The influx of reported incidents strains the team’s ability to respond to the reported
locations in a timely manner, many of which are recurring areas that are tagged soon
after removal. The Landscape Section is currently recruiting three additional part-time
staff to join the Graffiti team to assist with this inundation, but upgraded equipment is
still needed.

In May and November 2023, to help address the ongoing problem and improve program
efficiencies, the City purchased and put into service two similar specialized graffiti
removal trucks. However, one technician continues to utilize outdated vehicles and
equipment, which requires towing a pressure washer trailer with two gasoline-powered,
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Req. No. 240740 with Warren-Anderson Ford, Inc.
February 7, 2024
Page 2

airless paint pumps. This operation is cumbersome and makes maneuvering in tight
spaces difficult. This type of equipment must continually be cleaned and maintained
between uses, resulting in decreased response times. Adding a third graffiti removal
truck will outfit all program technicians with safer, more efficient equipment to streamline
operations, increase production, and improve response time.

DISCUSSION
Graffiti abatement is an integral part of keeping the City’s public areas safe and clean
while maintaining a high quality of life in our community. Therefore, it is essential to equip
staff with updated equipment to accomplish these goals.

In late 2023, staff were notified that Ventura County did not proceed with an F550 Graffiti
truck order originally ordered in 2020. This proposed Roadline Model GPMT Graffiti
Removal Truck will be fully equipped with up to four airless pumps and corresponding
airless spray guns connected by high-pressure lines of various lengths, contained by a
reel hose at the rear of the truck. A hot water high-pressure water blaster will rest on the
bed of the truck, which uses a cleaning solution to remove graffiti. Safety lights will be
installed to warn other vehicles and pedestrians about the truck. This addition to the fleet
will save the City on maintenance costs incurred from using older vehicles and equipment.
This truck will be ready for delivery and put into service in the first quarter of 2024.

The existing vehicles will remain in City inventory and will be used as a backup for graffiti
removal when needed and to support the Landscape Maintenance Division.

FISCAL IMPACT
$156,947; Funds for the purchase order with Warren-Anderson Ford, Inc. for one
Roadline Model GPMT Graffiti Removal Truck are budgeted in Measure AV equipment
capitalized (15733006-774400). Operating and maintenance costs are projected to be
approximately $10,800 annually. This includes fuel, lubricants, scheduled and
unscheduled maintenance, and parts.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-8659 with Jones Lang LaSalle (JLL), Incorporated for
  California Air Resources Board (CARB), Fleet Electrification and Microgrid
  Studies in the amount of $150,000 for a term of six months from the date of the
  Notice to Proceed; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute Agreement No. A-8659
  with Jones Lang LaSalle Incorporated (JLL), including minimal and/or non-
  substantial changes.

BACKGROUND
According to the California Air Resources Board (CARB), the transportation sector is the
single most significant contributor of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere.
They estimate that approximately 40% of statewide emissions are from the
transportation sector, with it being as high as 50% when refinery and production
emissions are factored in. In addition to statewide transportation efforts, State and Local
Government entities (such as the City of Palmdale) have greater electric energy
compliance requirements. For example, beginning on January 1, 2024, 50% of annual
vehicle purchases per year must be zero-emission vehicles (ZEV), and beginning on
January 1, 2027, 100% of vehicle purchases must be ZEV.

The City of Palmdale currently has over 200 vehicles in its fleet. The City’s transition to
lower-emission vehicles is underway, with 90 heavy-duty vehicles being transitioned to
ZEV. Additional battery electric and hydrogen vehicles are planned and coupled with
the required electrification of power tools (running on battery power).
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approval of Agreement No. A-8659
February 7, 2024
Page 2

Funding is being made available for microgrid projects, which could incorporate the
above-mentioned energy sources and operate independently of the grid in the case of
a power outage. A microgrid is a group of energy loads and resources acting as a single
entity in relation to the electrical grid. This allows the connected entities to have grid
connectivity but could also operate independently of the grid as needed.

DISCUSSION
Currently, the City’s Maintenance Yard can accommodate a small number of electrified
vehicles; however, the facility’s infrastructure would not be able to support the transition
to an all-ZEV fleet and battery-powered power tools. Therefore, the City must create a
plan to transition to its use of future energy sources. In addition, local businesses that
are large energy users must also find ways to address their energy needs, and the City’s
Community Choice Aggregation program, Energy for Palmdale’s Independent Choice
(EPIC), needs to find ways to address this issue.

In response to this issue, the City released a Request for Proposals (RFP) for a CARB
Fleet Electrification and Microgrid study. The RFP requested proposals for determining
the Maintenance Yard’s needs, how to best address the needs, and an outline of how the
successful bidder can perform future microgrid studies on behalf of EPIC and its
customers’ future needs.

The City received nine (9) proposal responses. After a detailed review by a City selection
committee, JLL was selected to perform the study. They will perform a study to determine
what the City’s fleet will look like as it transitions to an all-ZEV fleet in accordance with
CARB requirements, what the Maintenance Yard’s infrastructure needs to accommodate
the City’s future fleet, and how best to phase in the needed infrastructure. Additionally,
JLL may prepare proposals and quotes for future microgrid studies as needed by EPIC.

$150,000; The City has budgeted funding from an Energy Efficiency and Conservation
Block Grant (EECBG) in Account Number G0165241-724525-2420.

BETWEEN THE CITY OF PALMDALE AND JONES LANG LASALLE AMERICAS,

THIS CONTRACT FOR CONSULTANT SERVICES (“Contract” herein) is made and
entered into by and between the City of Palmdale a public body corporate and politic,
(hereinafter called “CITY”) and JONES LANG LASALLE AMERICAS, INC.
(hereinafter called “CONSULTANT”). This Contract shall become effective on the
date of the last signatory.

  RECITALS

  WHEREAS, City desires to engage CONSULTANT to provide certain
consultant services; and

  WHEREAS, CONSULTANT represents that CONSULTANT has the expertise
and is qualified to perform the services described in this Contract. And, if required, is
duly registered under the laws of the State of California; and

  WHEREAS, CONSULTANT desires to accept such engagement.

NOW, THEREFORE, the parties agree as follows:

1  DESCRIPTION OF WORK

1.1  The City hereby engages CONSULTANT, and CONSULTANT accepts such
engagement, to provide the following services:

a. High-Level Vehicle Conversion Review

Consultant will prepare a high-level analysis to identify a purchasing strategy for
transitioning the City’s fleet to a Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) fleet, including short-
term, medium-term, and long-term purchasing milestones. The analysis will provide a
high-level identification of vehicle replacement suitability from a technical and
financial perspective. Consultant will engage the City’s Fleet Maintenance
Superintendent and other appropriate personnel via a data validation and scenario-
building meeting to collaboratively identify key scenarios/needs to include in the fleet
assessment. The scenarios identified will integrate with the Consultant’s software,
EValuate™, to address their impact on the fleet transition strategy. Consultant will
recommend the most cost-effective ZEV options that meet the following operational
requirements:

• Vehicle Type – ZEV matches the vehicle type and weight for existing fleet vehicle.
Consultant will work with the City to determine if current vehicle use has any
operational flexibility that could lead to and expand range of potential vehicles,
optimizing total cost of operation (TCO).

  Concord - Document ID: generated after first signature  1-19
 • Range – ZEV range is sufficient to support the fleet vehicle’s daily range
requirement, accounting for reduced Electric Vehicle (EV) range in extreme climates.

• Charging and Refueling – EV, with recommended charger, can fully charge to meet
the daily range requirement during non-operating hours. Consultant will identify
appropriate methods to refuel a Hydrogen fueled vehicle.

Upon identifying the technical suitability of ZEV replacements, Consultant will use
EValuate™ to examine the financial suitability of transitioning the City’s fleet.
Consultant will work with the City to determine and adjust cost parameters it
considers financially suitable. Still, the baseline analysis will make recommendations
only where the ZEV TCO is estimated to be less than 100% of the TCO of a new ICE
vehicle. To make ZEV replacement recommendations, EValuate™ performs an
apple-to-apples comparison between ICE and ZEVs using preestablished financial
considerations. The factors are refined to capture the most accurate comparison for
the fleet, highlighting capital expenditure (CapEx) and operational expenditures
(OpEx) costs that impact the TCO.

b. Filing for Postponement

Based on the fleet conversion review results, Consultant will determine whether the
City can comply with the California Air Resources Board (CARB) Advanced Clean
Fleets regulation. This determination will be based on confirmation that the City
meets one of the eligible delay criteria: manufacturing and shipping of infrastructure
equipment, changes in general contractor, obtaining power/fuel, unexpected safety
issues during construction, discovery of archaeological/historical/tribal cultural
resources, natural disasters, utility cannot supply enough power to fleet owner site.
Consultant will engage directly with Southern California Edison (SCE) to understand if
the requisite electrical capacity to meet EV charging requirements can be provided in
time to meet the CARB requirements. Concurrently, Consultant will leverage its
network of over 80 EV charging and microgrid developers to gauge whether supply
chain issues could impact delivery of EV charging infrastructure and compliance with
CARB electrification requirements. This assessment will lead to recommendations for
any filings or actions with CARB or other entities to adjust electrification timelines.

c. Capacity Review

Consultant will use its collective engineering and design experience to provide a
comprehensive capacity review for the City’s Maintenance Yard. Consultant will
analyze the site’s existing electrical infrastructure for capacity to support charging
operations for the planned ZEV fleet and additional capacity for ancillary loads
beyond vehicle loads. Consultant will perform a load and forecasting analysis that
incorporates the impact of planned energy conservation measures, renovations, and

  Concord - Document ID: generated after first signature  2-19
 any new construction at the Maintenance Yard to establish a load profile for the site.
Concurrently, Consultant, will schedule and execute detailed site surveys to assess
the condition of existing infrastructure and the feasibility of utility or City distribution
infrastructure upgrades. Using the collected information, Consultant will perform
preliminary power system analyses, including power flow and short circuit studies, to
identify any grid integration challenges, voltage regulation, system capabilities, and
potential infrastructure system upgrades needed to meet the utility or onsite
distribution electrical system needs to incorporate solar. Consultant will identify red-
flags and major cost drivers early on in project development and capture the data
within the comparison of alternative solutions so that the City can make the most
informed investment prioritizations.

d. Technology Review

Consultant will perform a Microgrid technology review for the Maintenance Yard site,
capturing a concept intended to meet the maximum expected load from the charging
needs and the ability to use the Microgrid in use cases. Consultant will review Battery
Energy Storage Systems (BESS), renewable and fuel-burning energy generation
options, hydrogen, and backup energy options. The team will include site visits as
necessary into the surveys, as well as using aerial, satellite, and street-view pictures
to measure available site space adequately. Consultant will review multiple Microgrid
configurations with various technologies using a distributed generation optimization
software, HOMER Grid, to model different dispatching use cases. The use cases will
be designed to meet the maximum expected load as well as provide options for the
City to use in different scenarios for potential economic payback. Use cases will
assess the incorporation of single and/or multiple loads as well as the following:

• Peak Shaving – Energy storage provides energy cost avoidance on utility bills,
charging during hours with low cost or usage and discharging during hours with high
cost or usage.

• Energy Resilience – Onsite energy enables additional resilience benefits such as
back-up power for minutes or hours in the case of an outage.

• Load Shifting – Energy storage can also provide energy cost avoidance through
load shifting with similar intention and benefit as peak shaving.

• Renewable Production Shifting – Pairing energy storage with solar also allows the
battery to shift excess solar production in situations where net metering is unavailable
or has a low financial incentive or to firm up the peak shaving ability of the solar. In
these scenarios, the battery provides power conditioning, frequency regulation,
manages the intermittency of solar production, and provides some energy storage
during times with no to minimal solar production.

  Concord - Document ID: generated after first signature  3-19
 • Carbon arbitrage – Energy storage can also help lower emissions from the grid by
performing carbon arbitrage; shifting electric consumption from high emissions

e. Needs Assessment and Gap Analysis

After the capacity review and initial conceptual layouts have been created, Consultant
will leverage the work to identify the necessary charging stations to meet the City’s
electrification goals and provide a gaps analysis for the current electrical
infrastructure at the Maintenance Yard to identify any system augmentation
necessary to accommodate the new EV charging and microgrid infrastructure.

After completing the needs assessment and gaps analysis, Consultant will build out
capital cost estimates for the proposed configurations to meet the City’s vehicle
electrification and charging goals. Consultant will use HOMER Grid to develop a
granular definition of investments and savings through an optimization of equipment
sizing and operational dispatch of energy assets. This will inform an iterative
approach to cost estimating that allows for efficient assessment of technology
opportunities and more refined cost estimates as prioritized projects are defined.
Consultant will leverage validated cost information from its vast network of vendors
and developers, and actual cost data from implementing comparable projects.

Consultant will evaluate various incentive and credits-based programs to maximize
the potential cost savings in the capital cost estimates, such as applicable California
rebates, investment tax credits, cost savings, Renewable Energy Certificate (REC)
revenue programs, the CA Microgrid Incentive Program, and the Inflation Reduction
Act (IRA) direct pay option for any solar installation options. Consultant will determine
the cost-effectiveness and application of each program based on the City’s risk
appetite and potential impacts to operations. Consultant will build out a cost estimate
for the EV charging infrastructure, Microgrid configurations, and any infrastructure
upgrades necessary to install the proposed systems. The components considered in
each estimate are listed below:

• Capital cost estimates
• EV Charging equipment
• Microgrid assets (Solar, BESS, fuel-burning generation)
• Site backup/black-start generation

City’s fleet electrification plan and develop financial models that compare the costs
and benefits of various charging infrastructure ownership models, including but not

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council approve the City’s 2024 State and Federal
Legislative Platform (Legislative Platform) to promote Palmdale’s legislative priorities.

BACKGROUND
Active legislative engagement is necessary to protect and enhance the interests of
Palmdale’s residents and businesses. The City Council has identified the importance of
having an approved and current Legislative Platform to improve the organization’s
legislative efficiency and effectiveness. The City Council last approved the City’s
Legislative Platform on February 5, 2019.

DISCUSSION
Approving an updated Legislative Platform provides the framework to continue
addressing the fundamental issues deemed by the City Council as imperative to the City
and community while delivering a proactive approach to deal with the rapidly changing
nature of state and federal legislative and policy issues. The development of the
Legislative Platform allows for a guiding blueprint to engage in proactive advocacy efforts
at the state and federal levels. The Legislative Platform will form a cornerstone of the
City’s advocacy and legislative priorities in four strategic areas that staff will utilize to
advance City initiatives: Building Culture & Community, Economic Vitality & Innovation,
Social Unity, and Transportation & Infrastructure.

City staff works collaboratively with the City’s contracted state lobbying firm, Gonsalves
& Son, and federal lobbying firms, Lincoln Park Group, LLC and Townsend Public Affairs,
Cal Cities (formerly League of California Cities), and the California Contract Cities
Association (CCCA) to monitor and track legislation impacting local governments. These
advocacy teams work with the City and lawmakers to sponsor, draft, and support

  1
 INTRODUCTION

The Legislative Platform for the City of Palmdale was developed utilizing the City Council’s
goals and priorities, which apply to legislative priorities at both State and Federal levels of
government. These legislative priorities fall under the Council’s four strategic focus priority
areas that the City will work to advance in 2024 and beyond: Building Culture & Community,
Economic Vitality & Innovation, Social Unity and Transportation & Infrastructure.

The City strongly promotes local control of cities. It will support or oppose legislation based on
whether it impacts local control over City revenues, land use, community development, and
other municipal actions.

This document describes focus areas; however, due to the vigorous nature of the policy-
making process, additional issues are likely to arise throughout the legislative session. The
overarching principles in this Legislative Platform shall guide and direct staff as these different
issues require action. Any policy issues not addressed in this platform will be communicated to
the City Council for consideration before the City acts on that item.

  2
   BUILDING CULTURE & COMMUNITY
The City of Palmdale seeks resources and tools to promote the safety of our
residents, uplift community pride through beautification programs and elevate the
community’s preparedness and resiliency.

WE SUPPORT

Beautification, Public Appearance and Environmental Health
 Support all legislation that furthers the expansion and development of tools and programs
  to deter crimes of vandalism, graffiti and illegal dumping, and investment in the aesthetics
  and physical environment of the City, including but not limited to Landscape Maintenance
  Districts (LMDs), trees, hardscapes and public art.

Public Safety
 Work with federal, state, county, and regional agencies to further legislation intended to
  facilitate public safety; to support funding through grants and other opportunities to
  enhance community-oriented policing policies and programs in the City aimed at reducing
  crime and increasing social trust; and support the development of programs that enhance
  relationship-building between law enforcement and Palmdale youth.

Emergency Preparedness
 Support federal and state legislation providing funding through grants and other
  opportunities for emergency operations, hazard mitigation, and emergency response and
  recovery from natural and unnatural disasters.

Housing Improvement and Availability Program

 Support legislation that promotes, enhances, and funds the development of programs to
  encourage and assist in maintaining quality housing standards and availability to all.
  Likewise, oppose all measures that limit, impair, or dilute the City’s ability to address these
  issues.

Housing and Land Use Development

 Support legislation that allows the City to have local control to address the community's
  broadest and least regulated economic, land use, environmental, and permitting needs
  while expanding opportunities to build affordable housing and transit-oriented
  developments.

  3
 WE OPPOSE

Efforts to reprioritize public safety funding and programs

 Oppose efforts to reprioritize public safety funding and programs without proper procedural
  or stakeholder engagement and measures that would decrease public safety services or
  increase crime.

Loss of local control

 Oppose state initiatives that would remove local control, allow for irresponsible housing
  development in Palmdale and its spheres of influence, and interfere with protecting
  residential neighborhoods.

Unrealistic Timeframes

 Oppose new legislation and mandates for unrealistic processing timeframes or conditions
  that impede housing for larger housing development projects.

Imposition of Regulatory or Statutory Requirements

 Oppose legislation that affects and impairs the administration of parks and recreation
  services and resources management, including the sale of parklands and open space and
  relaxations of park dedication fee requirements that provide no added protections or
  benefits to California’s recreational consumer.

 Oppose any action in opposition to issues the City supports.

  4
   ECONOMIC VITALITY & INNOVATION
The City of Palmdale supports activities and opportunities that will help develop a
skilled workforce and grow the local economy through innovative programs and
incentives, including expanding the film and industrial/manufacturing industries in
the local region.

WE SUPPORT

Local Jobs

 Legislation that assists and creates comprehensive economic development strategies to
  create local jobs, including mortgage-paying jobs, by targeting growing industries, including
  film, healthcare, manufacturing, industrial and warehousing, and technology testing
  facilities.

Workforce Development

 Support legislation that supports funding and initiatives that encourage and support the
  growth of workforce development, skill development, and training opportunities in the City
  and region.

 Support legislation that expands workforce development programs that encourage diversity
  in business industries serving Palmdale.

Small Business Development

 Seek and support legislation that promotes financial support through grants and other
  funding opportunities to support and educate small businesses.

Economic Development Investment Incentive Programs

 Advocate for legislation that expands resources that modernizes existing economic
  development programs, including Enhanced Infrastructure Financing Districts (EIFD).

Film & Tourism

 Support and initiate legislation to enhance the economy and create jobs in all creative
  industries, especially film and tourism opportunities.

Exploring New Industries

 Advocate for legislation that proposes and enhances programs and funding to create jobs
  and develop a workforce in high-tech innovation and green technology industries.

  5
 WE OPPOSE

By-right legislation

 Oppose legislation that limits the City’s discretionary review processes for local
  development projects or economic development opportunities.

 Oppose legislation that interferes, limits, or eliminates the decision-making authority of local
  municipalities regarding local land use or economic development opportunities.

Unfunded Mandates

 Oppose the imposition of unfunded or less-than-funded mandates on local governments,
  regardless of the form, source, or policy, including administrative, legislative, and
  interpretive sources, regardless of the governmental or other source.

  6
   SOCIAL UNITY
The City of Palmdale seeks funding and supports opportunities to maximize
sustainability initiatives that address connectivity, homelessness and mental
health, public accessibility, and environmental sustainability.

WE SUPPORT

Broadband

 Support legislation supporting funding to advance Broadband City-wide to all residents
  regardless of income status.

Environmental Sustainability

 Support legislation supporting funding for clean transportation, net zero energy use in
  future construction projects, and a localized organics treatment facility.

Housing

 Support legislation supporting increased funding through administrative and housing
  programs that create diverse housing options in Palmdale, including affordable, veterans,
  low-income, senior, and workforce housing.

SAVES Program

 Advocate for legislation funding resources for the South Antelope Valley Emergency
  Services (SAVES) program.

Homelessness and Mental Health

 Support legislation enhancing regional and City-driven solutions to address homelessness
  through crisis response, mental health evaluation and treatment, housing, homeless
  outreach teams, and state and regional funding for mental health crisis units.

 Support legislation providing for the expansion of conservatorship laws, allowing for
  increased guardianship control and health supervision of those with mental illness and
  recognizing mental illness and addiction as a contributor to chronic homelessness.

Domestic Violence Programs

 Support legislation providing funding through grants and other opportunities to address
  domestic violence issues, including funding for the development of shelter and program
  services.

  7
 Illegal Drug Prevention and Treatment

 Support legislation funding programs targeting the education, prevention, and treatment of
  the use of illegal drugs and legal drug misuse.

Public Accessibility

 Support legislation funding through grants and other opportunities that enhance public
  facilities and programs, including recreational trails, parks, libraries, and museums, to make
  them accessible to all populations.

WE OPPOSE

Regional Housing Need Assessment (RHNA) Mandate

 Oppose legislation that proposes to change the Regional Housing Need Assessment
  (RHNA) from a planning process to a production requirement.

 Oppose legislation that penalizes a city or local government if identifiable RHNA units are
  not constructed or are delayed by actions of third parties.

  8
   TRANSPORTATION & INFRASTRUCTURE
Palmdale seeks funding and opportunities to promote the transformation of transit,
water, and technological advancements in our community.

WE SUPPORT

High Desert Corridor Alignment

 Support the implementation and construction of the High Desert Corridor Alignment project
  and support or initiate legislation to advance the same.

Palmdale Airport Development

 Vigorously support the mission of Air Force Plant 42 while concurrently working with local,
  state, and federal agencies to bring commercial passenger air service to the Palmdale
  Airport.

Recycled Water Infrastructure

 Support the development of recycled water infrastructure throughout the City and initiate
  legislation to further the same.

Technology Infrastructure

 Support legislation and policies oriented toward advancing and constructing technology
  infrastructure throughout the City, including broadband and wireless communications that
  support Smart Cities initiatives.

 Support or initiate legislation and policies furthering local oversight and control of
  technology placement and franchises.

Palmdale Boulevard

 Support legislation and administrative efforts that seek funding for the acquisition of
  Palmdale Boulevard from CalTrans.

Avenue M Grade Separation

 Support legislation and administrative efforts that seek funding for the Avenue M Grade
  Separation project.

  9
 Rancho Vista Grade Separation

 Support legislation and administrative efforts that seek funding for the Rancho Vista Grade
  Separation project and advocate for partnership with the Federal Railroad Administration to
  implement the project.

Hydrogen Infrastructure

 Support infrastructure legislation and funding opportunities for investments in green energy
  projects, including hydrogen refueling infrastructure, to decrease the City’s carbon footprint
  while not being destructive to small businesses and the local economy.

Rail Infrastructure

 Support expansion and construction of high-speed rail infrastructure, including the
  California High-Speed Rail project and Brightline, and develop a strategy to prepare the
  local economy for project deployment.

WE OPPOSE

Regulation of Wireless Facilities

 Oppose any legislation or regulatory policy that limits local discretion to regulate wireless
  facilities, cellular communications towers, transmission sites, or other infrastructure.

 Oppose any legislation or administrative policy that opposes any City goal, initiative, or
  policy.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Receive public testimony regarding proposed Resolution No. CC 2024-017;

  2. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-017 denying Appeal 24-0002; and,

  3. Find that the request is exempt from environmental review.

BACKGROUND

Project Description: Renaissance Holdings, LLC and Land Developers and Associates
are requesting City Council approval of Appeal (APP) 24-0002, overturning the Planning
Commission’s decision to deny General Plan Amendment (GPA) 23-0001, Zone
Change (ZC) 23-0002, and Specific Plan Amendment (SPA) 22-001. The proposed
requests include an amendment to the Antelope Valley Auto Center Specific Plan (SP)
boundary for the removal of seven parcels, totaling approximately 20 acres and
modifying the General Plan Land Use designation and Zone of those seven parcels from
SP to Regional Commercial (RC). There is no development proposed at this time and
future development would require separate review and approval.

In addition, the appellant is disputing the fees associated with the appeal application and
is requesting a refund of $1,512.75.

On January 11, 2024, the Planning Commission adopted Resolution No. PC-2024-001
(Attachment 2), denying the proposed requests. An appeal of the decision was
submitted on January 22, 2024 (APP 24-0002), and scheduled for the February 7, 2024,
City Council meeting.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Reso No. CC 2024-017
February 7, 2024
Page 2

The SP was adopted on February 9, 1989, to guide the development of the Antelope
Valley Auto Center (also referred to as the Palmdale Auto Mall), a master-planned
automotive sales and leasing center designed to accommodate up to 15 auto
dealerships. Since 1989, there have been five amendments to the SP, not including the
proposed Specific Plan Amendment. The SP area is bounded by Technology Drive to
the north, State Route 14 to the east, Avenue Q to the south, and 5th Street West to the
west. The SP facilitated a unified environment through the coordinated use of similar
elements such as roundabouts, landscaping treatments, etc., which gives the Palmdale
Auto Mall a specific identity.

  FIGURE 1 – AERIAL MAP

The auto dealerships make a conscious economic decision to cluster to efficiently share
the market with their competitors. The design of the Palmdale Auto Mall created a
defined route for customers to shop for vehicles. Additionally, the design allows
dealerships to utilize the interior avenues (i.e., Auto Center Drive and Carriage Way)
onto which they front or face as their dealer storefronts. As shown in Figure 2, the
Palmdale Auto Mall currently has a total of eight auto dealerships, with the intention to
accommodate a total of 15.

DISCUSSION

SPA 22-001 has been initiated by the applicant to revise the SP boundary along the
southeastern portion of the SP for the removal of seven parcels, as shown in Figure 3.
With the modification to the SP boundary, GPA 23-0001 and ZC 23-0002 is a request to
amend the General Plan Land Use designation and zone of the seven parcels from SP
to RC. The proposed amendment would permit all the uses allowed within the RC zone
pursuant to Palmdale Municipal Code Table 17.47.020-1 (Allowed Uses –
Commercial/Office Zones).

The RC General Plan Land Use and Zoning designation is intended to accommodate
commercial/retail and service uses attracting consumers from a regional market area. RC
areas provide access to long-term goods and services such as big box retailers. However,
the RC General Plan Land Use and Zoning designation does not allow new or used
vehicle sales. The Palmdale Auto Mall is the only location throughout the City that allows
the commercial sale of automobiles, and removing the seven parcels from the SP would
prevent the expansion of the Palmdale Auto Mall if a new dealership wants to locate in
Palmdale. Additionally, the area is currently able to support commercial/retail uses to the
west and south of the SP. Furthermore, no development is proposed in conjunction with
this request.

  SECTION 1. The City Council hereby specifically finds that all of the facts set

   SECTION 2. The City Council hereby finds as follows with respect to the
environmental documentation:
  (a)  APP 24-0002 is exempt from the requirements of the California
  Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines. The proposed application
  is subject to the “general rule” exemption pursuant to California
  Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3), which
  provides that, where it can be seen with certainty that there is no
  possibility that the activity in question may have a significant effect on the
  environment, the activity is not subject to CEQA. The proposed
  Application involves the appeal of a decision to deny changing the
  boundary of a SP, Land Use map and Zoning map and, therefore, is not
  subject to CEQA. Additionally, given that the request does not include any
  development, it does not result in a physical change that could cause an
  impact to the environment. Any future development application would be
  reviewed for CEQA compliance under a separate entitlement and the
  appropriate environmental document shall be prepared to address project-
  specific impacts. Therefore, the appeal will not have a significant effect on
  the environment.

  (b)  The custodian of records for the environmental document, and all other
  materials which constitute the record of proceedings upon which the City
  Council’s decision is based, is the Planning Manager of the City of
  Palmdale. These documents are available for public review in the
  Planning Division of the City of Palmdale located at 38250 Sierra
  Highway, Palmdale, California 93550, telephone (661) 267-5200.

  SECTION 3. Based upon substantial evidence presented to the City Council
during the February 7, 2024, public hearing, including public testimony and written and
oral staff report, the City Council specifically finds as follows:

  (a)  The proposed change in land use is consistent with State law. (GPA)

  (b)  The proposed Zone Change is consistent with the goals, policies, and
  objectives of the General Plan. (ZC)

  (c)  The distribution, location, and extent of land uses, including open space,
  as depicted in the Specific Plan is consistent with the General Plan. (SPA)

  APP 24-0002 is a request to overturn the Planning Commission’s decision
  to deny GPA 23-0001, ZC 23-0002, and SPA 22-001.
   The proposed requests include an amendment to the SP boundary for the
  removal of seven parcels, totaling approximately 20 acres, and modifying
  the General Plan Land Use designation and Zone of those seven parcels
  from SP to Regional Commercial (RC). The request is not consistent with
  applicable goals, policies and objectives of the SP and therefore the
  applicant is requesting a SPA in conjunction with the GPA and ZC. There
  is no development proposed at this time and future development would
  require separate review and approval. In addition, the General Plan may
  only be amended four times per year and this amendment constitutes the
  first of 2024.

(d)  The amendment is reasonable and beneficial. (GPA)

(e)  The proposed Zone Change will not have a substantial adverse effect on
  surrounding properties or the community in general. (ZC)

  The approval of APP 24-0002 will have a substantial adverse effect on
  surrounding properties and the Palmdale Auto Mall community because it
  will modify the boundary of the SP to remove seven parcels along the
  southeastern portion of the SP as well as redesignate the General Plan
  Land Use and zone of those parcels from SP to RC as depicted in
  Exhibit C. Additionally, the amendment is not reasonable and will not be
  beneficial because the purpose of the SP was set forth to establish an
  automobile shopping center with ancillary and coordinated commercial
  sales, services, and uses. The proposed appeal would permit all uses
  allowed within the RC zone pursuant to Palmdale Municipal Code Table
  17.47.020-1 (Allowed Uses – Commercial/Office Zones). The RC General
  Plan Land Use and Zoning designation is intended to accommodate
  commercial/retail and service uses attracting consumers from a regional
  market area. RC areas provide access to long-term goods and services
  such as big box retailers. However, the RC General Plan Land Use and
  Zoning designation does not allow new or used vehicle sales. The
  Palmdale Auto Mall is the only location throughout the City that allows the
  commercial sale of automobiles, and removing the seven parcels from the
  SP would prevent the expansion of the Palmdale Auto Mall if a new
  dealership wants to locate in Palmdale. Furthermore, the auto dealerships
  make a conscious economic decision to cluster to efficiently share the
  market with their competitors. The Palmdale Auto Mall design created a
  defined route for customers to shop for vehicles. The design allows
  dealerships to utilize the interior avenues (i.e., Auto Center Drive and
  Carriage Way) onto which they front or face as their dealer storefronts.
  The Palmdale Auto Mall currently has a total of eight auto dealerships,
  with the intention of the SP to accommodate a total of 15.
   (f)  The Specific Plan provides for adequate public infrastructure and services
  needed to support the land uses described in the plan. (SPA)

  (g)  The standards and development criteria will ensure that development
  proceeds in an orderly fashion and maintains a high level of quality. (SPA)

  (h)  The Specific Plan contains implementation measures to ensure that
  development is supported by adequate infrastructure as development
  occurs. (SPA)

  (i)  The site is suitable for the type and intensity of development proposed.
  (SPA)

  (j)  The flexibility in development standards afforded by the Specific Plan
  process has resulted in a project providing a superior design and greater
  amenities than would occur pursuant to more traditional zoning practices,
  and the project provides clear and substantial benefit to the City. (SPA)

  No development was proposed in conjunction with the requests of GPA
  23-0001, ZC 23-0002, and SPA 22-001; therefore, the applications have
  not provided a superior design and do not provide a clear and substantial
  benefit to the City.

  SECTION 4. Based on the findings and conclusions set forth in the above
Sections, and based on all other evidence in the record, the City Council hereby adopts
Resolution No. CC 2024-017, denying APP 24-0002 and upholding Planning
Commission Resolution No. PC-2024-001 to deny GPA 23-0001, ZC 23-0002, and SPA
22-001 and deny the request for refund of application fees.

 SECTION 1.0  INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND
 1.0  INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND

  1.1  Purpose of the Specific Plan

  The Auto Center Specific plan is prepared pursuant to California
  Government Code Section 65450 et. Sep. The law requires that the Specific
  Plan contain a detailed program for the “systematic implementation of the
  General Plan” accomplished through the use of text and diagrams which
  detail the following:

  •  The distribution and extent of land uses;

  •  The distribution and extent of infrastructure;

  •  Standards for development and conservation resources where
  appropriate; and

  •  Statement of the relationship between the Specific Plan and the
  General Plan.

  To that end, it is the intent of this document to set forth the policies and
  standards that will regulate the construction of new auto dealership facilities
  within the Antelope Valley Auto Center.

  It is further the intent of the Specific Plan to define the criteria for
  implementing coordinated design and the overall visual identity of the
  center; while preserving the opportunity for individual creativity within each
  dealership project.

  1.2  Objectives of the Specific Plan

  The basic objectives of the Specific Plan are to:

  A. Establish a regional commercial automobile shopping center with
  ancillary and coordinated commercial sales, services, and uses;

  B. Establish cooperation and coordination, between the City of Palmdale
  and the Auto Center participants.

  2
   C. Establish a long term and on-going source of economic strength to the
  community in terms of employment and government revenue;

  D. Protect and enhance the natural, social, and physical attributes of the
  development area so as not to detrimentally affect adjacent existing
  developments; and

  E. Establish innovative and quality site planning and architectural design
  maintaining a prosperous and marketable specialized commercial
  complex unique and individual in itself.

1.3  Relationship to Other Plans

  The Auto Center Specific Plan represents roughly 12% of the commercial
  property located within proposed 10th Street West Assessment District (88-
  1). The Assessment District is being formed for the expressed purpose of
  upgrading the area’s sewer, water, roadway, and storm drain facilities to a
  level capable of supporting the planned regional commercial development.

  In addition to the Auto Center proposal, 100 acres within Assessment
  District 88-1 have currently been committed to a Regional Shopping Mall.
  Ground breaking is expected to begin in April of 1989.

1.4  Legislative Context

  The Auto Center Specific Plan is adopted in order to establish regulations,
  conditions, standards, and criteria for the implementation of a regional
  commercial shopping center providing automobile and related merchandise
  and services exclusively.

  When adopted, the Specific Plan will serve to implement the City of
  Palmdale Community General Plan. The Auto Center Specific Plan
  implements the goals and objectives of the Palmdale Community General
  Plan by:

  3
 A. Encouraging the economic fortitude of the community through long term
  commitment of high sales tax generating commercial uses to the project
  area;

B. Promoting the logical extension of urban services to an area planned
  for future regional commercial development; and

C. Advancing the aesthetic objectives of the community through ensuring
  high quality architectural and landscape design.

The objectives and standards outlined within the Auto Center Specific Plan
are necessary to ensure the integrity of the Auto Center concept. Once
confirmed, the Auto Center Specific Plan will serve as the regulatory statute
for the Auto Center. All requirements of the Zoning Ordinance and of the
specific zoning of the subject property must be complied with unless
alternative requirements are set forth in the Specific Plan. In the event the
Specific Plan fails to address certain standards, the City ordinances will
apply.

 SECTION 2.0  SPECIFIC DEVELOPMENT PLAN
 2.0  SPECIFIC DEVELOPMENT PLAN

  2.1  Project Description

  The Auto Center Specific Plan consists of 78 acres 43 acres and is located
  west of the Antelope Valley Freeway, in the City of Palmdale, California.
  (SPA 04- 01, adopted by City Council January 10, 2005.)(SPA 22-001 adopted by City
  Council XX,XX, 202X)

  The Auto Center Specific Plan allows for the construction of the Antelope
  Valley Auto Center, a master planned retail automotive sales and leasing
  center planned to accommodate up to 15 12 auto dealership franchises.
  (SPA 22-001 adopted by City Council XX.XX, 202X)

  Dealerships within the Auto Center are focused towards interior parking and
  circulation elements. The design is intended to create a synergism within
  the center where the success of one dealership promotes the success of
  another.

  It is the intent of the Specific Plan to ensure the creation of a unified
  environment through the coordinated use of similar elements which give the
  auto center a single identity. As with an enclosed shopping mall, the overall
  identity belongs to the mall itself. Individual vendors then establish their own
  identities within the context of this fabric.

  The Auto Center design creates a well-defined route for customers on which
  to shop with convenient parking area that allow them to feel free to walk in
  and out of the Dealers’ lots. The “mall” concept utilized the major interior
  avenues onto which the Dealerships front or face as their “store fronts”.
  These avenues include “roundabouts” at their intersections.

  The four major entrances off Technology Drive, 5th Street West and Avenue
  Q, one major and three minor, will be identified for visitors by signage. The
  project incorporates perimeter walls, to provide screening of storage and
  service areas at the rear of the properties. (SPA 04-01, adopted by City Council
  January 10, 2005.)

  It is intended that no particular “style” or period of architecture be replicated
  or copied in the design of any individual dealership buildings. That is, no
  building should be identifiably Spanish, Mediterranean, Santa Fe, High
  Tech, etc. Within the constraints outlined in this Specific Plan, each building
  should be thoughtfully designed to fit within the spirit of the

  6
   design concept and the environment. The architectural standards for the
  center are outlined in greater detail in the Architectural Design Manual to be
  submitted to the Director of Planning for his review and approval prior to the
  issuance of the first building permit for the center.

2.2  Environmental Setting

  The project site is vacant and undeveloped. Only sparse desert scrub
  covers the site and much of the vegetation has been destroyed by vehicular
  traffic which traverses the property on unimproved access roads.

  The project site gently slopes to the northeast and is topographically flat,
  with elevations ranging between 2,640 and 2,680 feet.

  The properties surrounding the project site are predominantly vacant. The
  Antelope Valley Freeway (State Route 14) borders the site on the east.
  South of Avenue Q, a three-story hotel complex has been constructed and
  west of the project on the northwest corner of 5th Street West and Avenue
  Q is an existing union meeting hall. The remaining properties surrounding
  the project site are vacant at this time.

2.3  Community Setting

  The City of Palmdale is one of the fastest growing cities of the State of
  California. Current population figures estimate the combined population of
  the Cities of Lancaster and Palmdale and the community of Quartz Hill at
  147,367 persons. The 1990 projections estimate the population of these
  communities at 214,964 persons.

  Rapid residential growth in the last six years has triggered an increase in
  demand for public services. Recognizing the need to generate additional
  revenues to support increased demand, the City of Palmdale
  Redevelopment Agency set forth to establish Redevelopment Project areas
  within which tax increment could be collected to finance infrastructure and
  encourage upgrades to blighted areas. The Auto Center Specific Plan area
  is located within Redevelopment Project No. 4 which was adopted under
  Ordinance 515 on November 10, 1983 by the City of Palmdale Community
  Redevelopment Agency.

 2.4  Development Plan

  A. Purpose

  The primary purpose of the Auto Center Specific Plan is to implement
  the General Plan through the physical and economic development of
  78 acres59 acres of commercial property located within Redevelopment
  Project Area No. 4. It is further the purpose of this development plan to
  promote Auto Center uses and to encourage the highest and best
  quality of design and environment within the designated area. (SPA 04-
  01, adopted by City Council January 10, 2005). (SPA 22-001, adopted by City Council
  XX,XX, 202X)

  B. Plan Design Policies

  1. New car showrooms shall be developed under a coordinated design
  concept orienting facilities towards pedestrian travel areas and
  parking nodes.

  2. Design of signs, landscaping, and lighting shall provide an attractive
  environment to Auto Center visitors and employees, as well as
  motorists on the freeway and neighboring properties.

  3. Aesthetically pleasing entrances to the development area shall be
  established through the implementation of design and development
  standards contained herein.

  4. Automobile display and storage facilities shall be enhanced through
  the use of a coordinated landscape street design.

  5. Design theme of buildings, landscaping, and all site improvements
  shall be integrated to comprise a unified motif throughout the
  development area.

  6. Development characteristics which result in a visual or audible
  nuisance to the development shall be prohibited.

  8
 9
 10
   7. Ancillary uses to the primary use of the Auto Center shall be
  integrated into the plan provided that these facilities enhance the
  design efficiency and feasibility of the primary use.

  8. A Dealer’s Association shall be formed and comprised of lot owners
  and shall encourage cooperation in the development, maintenance,
  and marketing of services provided within the Auto Center.

  9. The project shall be designed so as to create a “sense of place”. This
  shall be accomplished through the use of dramatic landscaping,
  controlled signage, color, and architectural design.

  C. Land Use Designation/Use Zones

  All properties located within the Auto Center shall be designated as
  Specific Plan, consistent with the City of Palmdale Zoning Ordinance.
  The development standards contained within this Specific Plan shall be
  governing standards for development within the Center.

2.5  Circulation Element

  A. Purpose

  The purpose of the Circulation Element is to define the location and
  extent of roadway improvements within the Auto Center.

  B. Circulation Element Policies

  1. Safe and efficient access within the Auto Center for both vehicles
  and pedestrians is a priority of the Specific Plan.

  2. The circulation system shall be designed to be sensitive to
  surrounding land uses and shall contribute to the overall circulation
  in the project area.

  3. Roadway improvements shall be designed with sufficient right-of-
  way to support the level of services required by traffic generated from
  the Auto Center and surrounding areas.

  11
   4. An integrated landscape concept along the roadway shall be created
  to not only enhance community design but to provide security for the
  auto dealerships as well.

  5. On-site parking, adequate to accommodate one (1) space per
  employee at the largest shift, shall be provided for all dealerships.
  Employee parking areas may be constructed to be common to more
  than one dealership, however, in no event are employees allowed to
  park within the public road right-of-way for the Auto Center. Parking
  for customers shall be provided within the right-of-way and within the
  joint use parking nodes.

  6. Adequate area within the right-of-way must be provided to allow for
  the loading and unloading of vehicles. The roadways shall be
  designed with sufficient radius to accommodate the turning motions
  of automobile transport vehicles.

  7. Employer-sponsored transportation measures, such as ridesharing,
  carpool/vanpools, and preferential parking should be encouraged
  whenever possible.

  8. Individual dealers shall attempt to provide on-site loading and
  unloading of vehicles. If a public street is used for such activities,
  arrangements shall be made to avoid conflicts with customer
  visitations.

C. Circulation Element Concept

  The roadway standard utilized within the Auto Center Specific Plan
  varies according to location and area served. In all instances however,
  the standard is reflective of the Los Angeles County Road Department
  Standards Planning manual.

  The City of Palmdale has designated Avenue P-8 as a major highway.
  There has been discussion on constructing an off ramp at Avenue P-8.
  While these discussions have not progressed beyond the conceptual
  stage, the Auto Center Specific Plan is sensitive to the future need for
  right-of-way acquisition. An easement will be reserved for a future off
  ramp that will be located in the northeast corner of the project.

  The purpose of the Public Facilities Element is to define the location and

 2.7  Landscape Concept Element

  A. Purpose

  The purpose is to establish a comprehensive, attractive, and unified
  landscaped concept for the Antelope Valley Auto Center.

  B. Landscape Design Policies

  1.  The landscaping shall be designed to provide an attractive and
  unifying appearance for the Auto Center by utilizing plant
  materials to soften and add color to the hardscape.

  2.  Landscaping should provide the emphasis at entrances and
  interior roundabouts.

  3.  Plant materials and hardscape elements are to create a unified
  streetscape along the interior streets of the Auto Center as well
  as provide security for and pedestrian access onto the
  automobile display area.

  4.  Landscaping elements at the community edges are to positively
  integrate the Center into the neighborhood.

  5.  The design of the landscaping must utilize materials indigenous
  to the local environmental climate and drought resistant
  wherever possible.

  6.  Material selections must  take  into  account  long  term
  maintenance issues.

  7.  The landscape concept shall establish minimum performance
  standards and a listing of acceptable plant materials.

  20
 C. The Landscape Concept

  The landscape concept addresses special treatment for various zones
  yet provides an overall visual continuity. These zones or areas are the
  entrances, central drive, roundabouts, pylon sign area, the loop road
  and streetscape, the perimeter edges and the freeway edge, individual
  dealer entries, and optional windows. The design reflects a hierarchy
  and performance requirements of these elements.

  The entries are formal and punctuate the arrival.

  The central drive (Auto Center Drive) is identified by a palm row in the
  median terminating at the central round-about. The roundabouts feature
  the most effective plantings and feature spaces for product display.
  Rings of palms identify the roundabouts.

  The pylon sign area is specially landscaped to provide an interesting
  base for the sign and add an attractive eye-catcher at the freeway.

  The streetscape design at the interior roads should provide low
  maintenance landscaping with no irrigation problems to the automobile
  on display, security, and pedestrian access. All this is accomplished by
  a module of planters.

  The perimeter edges provide ten feet of landscaping. The design
  primarily includes indigenous desert materials.

  The individual dealer entries will be designed from a palette of
  prototypes that fit with the streetscape modules and provide an
  opportunity for trees and berm.

D. The developer shall install all landscaping and irrigation within the public
  right-of-way and within five feet (5’) of the dealer parcels, all landscaped
  Auto Center entries, landscaping in the roundabouts, and pylon sign
  area. Individual dealers will install landscaping on their parcels except
  the five feet (5’) referenced above. The five feet (5’) planter area plus
  the dealers; landscaping improvements will equal 5% of the improved
  parcel.

  The Antelope Valley Auto Center’s Dealer’s Association will maintain all
  landscaped areas within the Auto Center including public right-of-

  21
   ways, entries, planters, employee parking areas, and the pylon sign
  area.

  The City of Palmdale Landscape Maintenance District will maintain all
  landscaping on Avenue P-8 and Avenue Q. The developer will maintain
  all landscaping along 5th Street West.  A separate landscape
  maintenance district will be formed for this purpose.

2.8  Signage Concept Element

  A. Purpose

  The purpose of the Signage Concept Element is to establish a Planned
  Sign Program for all development located within the Auto Center
  Specific Plan. This Element speaks only to on-site signage
  requirements.

  B. Signage Concept Element Policies

  1.  It is the intent of the Specific Plan to control the location, size,
  type, and design of all signage within the Auto Center to ensure
  a unified appearance to the Center.

  2.  A Freeway Identification sign will be established for the purpose
  of attracting customers to the Auto Center. The sign shall be
  located so as to be seen from both north and south bound traffic
  and be designed to exhibit the architectural theme of the center.

  3.  All entrances into the Auto Center will be clearly identified with
  monument signs. These signage areas shall be appropriately
  landscaped.

  4.  Dealer identification signs shall be carefully controlled to convey
  a uniform sense of identity.

  22
   C. Signage Concept Element Overview

  Signage within the Auto Center is regulated in two areas; signage for
  the Auto Center itself and signage for the individual dealership. The
  signage for the Auto Center identification has been designed and
  illustrated in the development standards section of the Specific Plan.
  The Signage program for the individual dealerships is strictly controlled
  by the Design Standards and is limited to the placement of monument
  signs at each driveway entrance, one 20-foot-tall pylon sign per
  dealership, and two primary wall signs per product line. Dealerships
  abutting the freeway may place signs on the rear of buildings allowing
  for greater visibility.

2.9  Grading Concept Element

  A. The Grading Concept Element establishes a grading design for the
  maximum development of the Specific Plan area. The site is
  topographically flat and there are no landforms that should be preserved
  to maintain the character of the property. The primary purpose of the
  grading concept therefore is to elevate the property and to provide for
  maximum freeway visibility for the Auto Center and to provide for storm
  drainage.

  B. Grading Concept Element Policies

  The property shall be graded to enhance the visibility of the Auto Center
  and commercial properties located west of 5th Street West.

  automobiles or trucks not in association with a dealership that

  3. The sale of new vehicle parts and equipment;

  5. Automobile and truck renting and leasing, except that the total
  number of lots and acreage in the Specific Plan area that may
  be utilized for the renting and leasing of automobiles and trucks

  automobiles and trucks not in association with a dealership that

  sale of automobiles;

   7. The sale and repair of new van conversions, campers, motor

B. Other Uses

  It is recognized that certain other uses can be compatible with permitted
  uses of this Specific Plan, but it is the intent of this plan to restrict and
  control locations, site design, and activities of these compatible uses.
  Therefore, the following uses may be permitted in the Auto Center
  Specific Plan provided that it is found:

  1. That the requirements of the Specific Plan are met;

  2. The existing traffic and circulation system can accommodate the
  additional uses;

  3. The use is compatible with the appearance character and
  activities of the Auto Center;

  4. The use does not detract from the continuity and integrity of new

  5. A Conditional Use Permit shall first be obtained from the City of
